traveler: John von Neumann (Neumann János Lajos, margittai Neumann János)
title: The Double Enrollment: Budapest, the Institute, and the Architecture Named After Him
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: Budapest and the Patent of Nobility

stops.name: Budapest, birth in the Lipotvaros
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day; the street address of the apartment is not consistently given in the biographies, so the pin marks the family's known quarter rather than a verified door
stops.campa: In the Lipótváros quarter of Budapest, above the financial district, Miksa Neumann and Margit Kann have a son and name him János Lajos. He is the eldest of three brothers; Mihály and Miklós follow him. The father is a lawyer who has become an investment banker at the Magyar Jelzálog Hitelbank; the mother's people belong to the same assimilated Jewish haute bourgeoisie that runs the credit of the Dual Monarchy. The empire has fourteen years left. The boy will outlive it by forty.
suggested_refs: The Lipotvaros quarter of Budapest and the Neumann family apartment, address usually given as Bathory utca 26
sources: Bhattacharya, The Man from the Future (2021)

stops.name: Budapest, the emperor's patent of nobility
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: Franz Joseph, in the sixty-fifth year of his reign, elevates Miksa Neumann to the Hungarian nobility for services to the economy. The family takes the predicate margittai, of Margitta, and arms bearing three marguerites. No estate comes with it and no acre of land; the title is a formality bought by a class that has money and wants standing. The son will turn the Hungarian particle into a German von when he begins publishing from Berlin, and the world will know him by that half of it. Franz Joseph dies three years later, and the state that issued the patent does not outlast the war.
suggested_refs: The 1913 Hungarian patent of nobility granting the predicate margittai to the Neumann family

stops.name: Budapest, the Fasori gymnasium and Laszlo Ratz
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year of entry, 1914 (Wikipedia; MacTutor); month and day not documented and defaulted. An earlier compilation gave 1911, which is wrong
stops.campa: He enters the Lutheran gymnasium on Városligeti fasor, where the mathematics master László Rátz reads the boy inside a term, tells the father that the school cannot teach him, and arranges private university tutoring alongside the ordinary curriculum. Eugene Wigner is a year ahead of him in the same corridor and will write his obituary memoir forty-four years later. Edward Teller is of the same city and the same generation. Three of the men who will build the American bomb are schoolboys here.
suggested_refs: The Fasori Evangelikus Gimnazium, Varosligeti fasor 17-21, Budapest, still teaching
sources: Halmos, 'The Legend of John von Neumann' (1973)

stops.name: Vienna, the flight from Bela Kun
stops.date_confidence: tradition carried by the corpus and by general biography; no primary document for the flight was consulted in this session, and the month is a default
stops.campa: The Hungarian Soviet Republic under Béla Kun takes the banks, and the Neumanns leave for Vienna until it falls. The exile runs months rather than years, and the family returns to a Budapest under Horthy with the numerus clausus about to close the universities to Jews. Nothing in the boy's schooling is interrupted by any of it. He is fifteen, and he keeps for the rest of his life a flat contempt for the politics that emptied the apartment and for the men who thought it could be reasoned with.
suggested_refs: The Hungarian Soviet Republic of 1919 and the flight of the Budapest banking families to Vienna

stops.name: Budapest, the first paper, with Fekete
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1922 through MacTutor's biography of Michael Fekete, which dates the paper one year after the gymnasium was completed; frequently and wrongly given as 1921, which is the year he left school. Month and day not documented
stops.campa: Mihály Fekete, brought in as a tutor, publishes with the boy a paper on the location of the zeros of certain minimum polynomials. It is the first of about a hundred and fifty. He has left the gymnasium the year before holding the Eötvös prize as the best mathematician leaving school in Hungary, and he has already been told by his father that mathematics does not feed a man. The paper settles nothing about that argument. It establishes only that the argument will be had with someone who can already publish.
suggested_refs: Fekete and von Neumann, 'Uber die Lage der Nullstellen gewisser Minimum Polynome', 1922
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, biography of Michael Fekete
MacTutor History of Mathematics, biography of von Neumann

stops.name: Berlin, chemistry and the absent doctorate
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1921; the month is inferred from the academic calendar. A gathered version of this claim carried Budapest coordinates for a sentence whose own text says Berlin
stops.campa: The compromise his father extracts holds for five years. He matriculates in mathematics at the Pázmány Péter University in Budapest and does not attend it, appearing only to sit examinations. He enrols in chemistry at the University of Berlin and does attend, in the city where Einstein holds a chair and where he sits in on Erhard Schmidt's seminar. He is seventeen. Two doctorates are being pursued in two countries by a student resident in neither for most of the year, and both will finish on time.
suggested_refs: The Friedrich-Wilhelms-Universitat, Berlin, and Erhard Schmidt's seminar

stops.name: Zurich, the entrance examination at the ETH
stops.date_confidence: attested for September 1923; the day is not given in the sources consulted
stops.campa: He passes the entrance examination for the Eidgenössische Technische Hochschule in September and begins chemical engineering, the practical credential Miksa Neumann insisted on. George Pólya lectures here and will say for the rest of his life that von Neumann was the only student he was ever afraid of: mention an unsolved problem in a lecture, and the solution arrives after class on a slip of paper. Hermann Weyl is here too. The chemistry is done properly and the diploma is taken, and nobody watching is fooled about which subject he is in.
suggested_refs: The ETH Zurich chemical engineering diploma, 1926, and Polya's recollection of his student
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, quoting George Polya

stops.name: Budapest, the doctorate summa cum laude
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1926, with Macrae giving March; the day is not given
stops.campa: He returns to Budapest between terms and takes the final examinations for the mathematics doctorate summa cum laude, with minors in experimental physics and chemistry. The thesis axiomatises set theory and supplies the definition of ordinal number still in use: an ordinal is the set of the ordinals below it. In the same year the ETH gives him the chemical engineer's diploma. He is twenty-two, holds two degrees from two countries in two subjects, and has stopped pretending the chemistry was ever the point.
suggested_refs: The 1926 Budapest doctoral thesis on the axiomatisation of set theory

stops.name: Gottingen, the year with Hilbert
stops.date_confidence: attested for the academic year 1926-27 on a Rockefeller Foundation grant; the month is inferred. The coordinate is the corpus's canonical Gottingen pin, inherited byte-identical, and sits about 1.4 km west of the city centre; the disagreement with Wikipedia's 51.5333 / 9.9356 is recorded and not resolved
stops.campa: A Rockefeller Foundation grant sends him to Göttingen to work under David Hilbert, whose programme, to put the whole of mathematics on a finite axiomatic footing, is the reason he came. He works on foundations and on the new quantum theory at once and finds the second more tractable than the first. Robert Oppenheimer arrives in the same season and takes his doctorate here. Five years later Kurt Gödel will show that Hilbert's programme cannot be completed, and von Neumann is among the first men in the room to see it.
suggested_refs: Hilbert's Gottingen seminar, 1926-27, and the Rockefeller Foundation fellowship files
sources: Sigmund, Exact Thinking in Demented Times (2017)

stops.name: Berlin, the youngest Privatdozent
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day for the habilitation; the superlative about his age is Wikipedia's and is carried as attribution rather than as confirmation
stops.campa: He completes the habilitation and is admitted to lecture at the University of Berlin, the youngest man ever granted that standing there. He teaches set theory, quantum mechanics, and the foundations of mathematics to rooms that fill because of who stands at the front of them. In the same decade he proves the minimax theorem: in any finite two-person zero-sum game there is a value, and each player can guarantee it against any play by the other. He does not yet call this economics. Nobody does.
suggested_refs: The 1928 paper 'Zur Theorie der Gesellschaftsspiele', containing the minimax theorem

stops.name: Berlin, Metropolis and the machine city
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day for the Metropolis premiere; the juxtaposition with the December habilitation is the atlas's, and the men did not meet
stops.campa: Fritz Lang opens Metropolis at the Ufa-Palast am Zoo in January, a film about a city that runs on bodies fed into a machine, and Berlin argues about it for a year. In the same city and the same twelve months Johannes Itten teaches the body as a discipline, Rudolf Laban writes movement down in notation, and a Hungarian of twenty-three habilitates in December on the axioms underneath physics. Four buildings run one argument about bodies and machines, and none of the four knows the others are having it.
suggested_refs: The Ufa-Palast am Zoo premiere of Metropolis, 10 January 1927

stops.name: Hamburg, the last German post
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1929-30; month and day not documented and defaulted
stops.campa: He takes a Privatdozent post at Hamburg and calculates openly what the German universities look like from below: too many brilliant young men, too few chairs, a decade of waiting for a man in a hurry. Oswald Veblen writes from Princeton in the same season, offering a term of lectures to an American mathematics that has decided to buy itself a European faculty. He accepts, expecting to divide his years between two continents indefinitely. Hamburg is the last German post he ever holds.
suggested_refs: Oswald Veblen's Princeton recruiting correspondence with European mathematicians, 1929

stops.name: Budapest, the marriage to Mariette Kovesi
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day (Macrae). MacTutor's looser '1929' refers to the pre-departure period rather than to a competing wedding date, and the apparent contradiction between the two sources dissolves on inspection
stops.campa: He marries Mariette Kövesi in Budapest on the first day of the year, and is baptised Catholic to make the wedding possible, a conversion the biographies record without anyone claiming it was a conviction. The couple sail within weeks for a country neither has seen. He is twenty-six and holds three positions in three cities, none of which he intends to give up. Within four years he will hold one, on another continent, and the German ones will have been taken from men like him by statute.
suggested_refs: The Budapest marriage register entry for Mariette Kovesi and Janos Neumann, 1 January 1930

stops.name: Port of New York, the liner docks
stops.date_confidence: arrival in early 1930 attested; the month is a placeholder, and the pier is not documented in any source consulted, so the pin marks the general harbour
stops.campa: The liner comes up the Hudson and he lands at New York to take up a visiting lectureship, one of a wave of Europeans Oswald Veblen is pulling into Princeton before anyone in Germany believes the wave is necessary. The pier is not in the record. He keeps his Berlin and Hamburg standing, crosses twice a year, and treats the Atlantic as a commute. Four years of that remain before the crossing becomes one-way and the word for it changes from lectureship to refuge.
suggested_refs: The transatlantic passenger manifests of early 1930, New York arrivals

stops.name: Princeton, the old Fine Hall
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 1930 lectureship and the 1931 full professorship; the month is inferred from the academic year
stops.campa: He takes up the lectureship in mathematical physics in the Fine Hall a later generation renames Jones Hall, and in 1931 Princeton makes him a full professor. Paul Dirac spends the academic year 1934 in these same rooms; Wigner arrives from Budapest by way of Berlin to a joint appointment. The building is a common room with a fireplace and an inscription from Einstein over the mantel, and the mathematics gets done in armchairs. He is twenty-seven, and the American post is still, in his own mind, the second of his jobs.
stops.quote: Young man, in mathematics you don't understand things. You just get used to them.
stops.quote_source: Reported by Felix T. Smith of Stanford Research Institute in Gary Zukav, The Dancing Wu Li Masters (New York: Bantam, 1979), p. 208 n.; third-hand, and the original exchange is undated
suggested_refs: Old Fine Hall (Jones Hall), Princeton University, shared by the mathematics department and the young Institute

stops.name: Berlin, the foundations of quantum mechanics
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year of publication; month and day not documented and defaulted
stops.campa: Springer publishes Mathematische Grundlagen der Quantenmechanik, begun in Berlin and finished in Princeton. States are unit vectors in a Hilbert space, observables are self-adjoint operators, and Heisenberg's matrices and Schrödinger's waves turn out to be one theory written twice. Bohr and Einstein had argued the interpretation at Solvay in 1927; this book writes down what they were arguing about. French readers have it in 1946 and Spanish readers in 1949; English readers wait until 1955.
suggested_refs: Mathematische Grundlagen der Quantenmechanik, Springer 1932; Robert T. Beyer's English translation, Princeton 1955; Nicholas A. Wheeler's re-edited edition, Princeton 2018

stops.name: Princeton, one of the founding six
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year; month and day not documented and defaulted
stops.campa: Abraham Flexner's new Institute for Advanced Study opens with six professors of mathematics and no students, no laboratories, no teaching duties, and no curriculum. Einstein is one of the six and von Neumann, at twenty-nine, is the youngest. He takes the chair he will hold for twenty-four years and co-edits the Annals of Mathematics from it. In Germany that spring the civil service law is stripping Jewish academics of their posts; the Institute's recruiting and the Reich's dismissals are one event seen from two sides.
suggested_refs: The founding faculty of the Institute for Advanced Study, School of Mathematics, 1933

stops.name: New York, a daughter named Marina
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day. Two separate lenses of the gathered material placed this birth in Princeton; Wikipedia's entry for Marina von Neumann Whitman gives New York City, and New York is used
stops.campa: His only child is born in New York and named Marina; she will become an economist and sit on the Council of Economic Advisers. The marriage to Mariette is over within two years and eight months of the birth, and the divorce is entered in November 1937. Custody is arranged so that the daughter comes to her father at an age he specifies in advance, on the stated reasoning that the early years are not the ones he is any use for. Both parties keep to it. She publishes a memoir of him in 2012, fifty-five years after his death.
suggested_refs: Marina von Neumann Whitman's own memoir of her father, The Martian's Daughter (2012)

stops.name: Budapest, the marriage to Klara Dan
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: He returns to Budapest in the autumn and marries Klára Dán, out of his own circle in the same city, and brings her back across an Atlantic that has about ten months of peace left over it. The Bôcher Memorial Prize arrives in the same year, for the memoirs on almost periodic functions on groups. She will end her working life writing machine code for weapons calculations and preparing his last, unfinished book for the press. It is very nearly the last crossing he makes in this direction.
suggested_refs: The Bocher Memorial Prize of the American Mathematical Society, 1938

stops.name: Aberdeen Proving Ground, the arithmetic of things that go off
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1940 (Wikipedia, 'Ballistic Research Laboratory'; MacTutor). A gathered range beginning in 1937 is unsupported and contradicted its own chronology; month and day not documented
stops.campa: He is named to the Scientific Advisory Committee of the Ballistic Research Laboratories at Aberdeen Proving Ground, under the director Hermann Zornig, and begins the work that occupies him until he dies: shaped charges, shock waves, exterior ballistics. Hydrodynamics of the kind the army needs cannot be solved in closed form, and it is here that he starts to want machines. The Navy Bureau of Ordnance takes him the following year. The pure mathematics has about eighteen months left in his working week.
suggested_refs: The Scientific Advisory Committee of the Ballistic Research Laboratories, Aberdeen Proving Ground, from 1940
sources: Bhattacharya, The Man from the Future

stops.name: Los Alamos, the lens that squeezes a sphere
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1943; the month is a placeholder within that year
stops.campa: He arrives on the mesa as a consultant and is put on the hardest geometric problem in the place. A plutonium core will not detonate by being shot at itself; it has to be crushed inward by a shell of explosive shaped so that the shock arrives everywhere at once. He works the lens design in the same corridor as Fermi and Feynman, and Tony Skyrme comes with the British Mission in July 1944. Oppenheimer runs the site. Niels Bohr is on it under the name Nicholas Baker. Nobody here can say where they work.
stops.quote: Johnny von Neumann was the greatest mathematician around.
stops.quote_source: Richard Feynman, Surely You're Joking, Mr. Feynman! (New York: W. W. Norton, 1985); page number unconfirmed
suggested_refs: The implosion lens design work of the X Division, Los Alamos, 1943-45
sources: Rhodes, The Making of the Atomic Bomb (1986)

stops.name: Kyoto, first on the list
stops.date_confidence: attested for the Target Committee session of 10-11 May 1945; the pin is Kyoto, the city discussed, not the room the committee sat in
stops.campa: The Target Committee meets in Washington and at Los Alamos to choose the cities. Von Neumann sits on it and argues from the physics: pick a target whose surrounding hills will hold the blast and reflect it back, and burst the weapon in the air rather than on the ground, at a height his own calculations supply. Kyoto stands at the head of the list. Henry Stimson strikes Kyoto off, twice, and it is replaced. Forty-five years later Edward Witten takes the Fields Medal in the same city.
suggested_refs: Minutes of the Target Committee, second and third meetings, 10-11 and 28 May 1945
sources: Rhodes, The Making of the Atomic Bomb

stops.name: Trinity, the estimate spoken aloud
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day for the test and for his presence as an observer
stops.campa: He watches from the observation area at dawn on the sixteenth of July. He had entered five kilotons in the Los Alamos betting pool, an analytical estimate, and says on the spot that it was at least five thousand tons and probably a lot more. The yield is twenty-one. Fermi is on Compania Hill with his strips of dropped paper, doing the estimate that popular accounts keep handing to von Neumann; the method is Fermi's. Two men are on the same desert an hour apart, doing arithmetic at the same explosion.
suggested_refs: Trinity Site, Jornada del Muerto, New Mexico, and the Los Alamos yield betting pool
sources: Rhodes, The Making of the Atomic Bomb

stops.name: Philadelphia, the Moore School and the eighteen thousand tubes
stops.date_confidence: attested for the summer of 1944; the railway-platform meeting with Goldstine is a story told by the participants and is not carried by any document
stops.campa: Herman Goldstine, so the participants tell it, recognises him on a railway platform at Aberdeen and mentions the electronic machine going up in Philadelphia. He appears at the Moore School soon after. ENIAC is eighteen thousand vacuum tubes and is programmed by replugging cables, a job of days. Eckert and Mauchly are already designing a successor in which the instructions would live in the same store as the numbers. He joins the discussion in the summer and does not leave it again while he is alive.
suggested_refs: The ENIAC installation at the Moore School of Electrical Engineering, University of Pennsylvania

stops.name: Princeton, the Theory of Games and Economic Behavior
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year of publication; month and day not documented and defaulted
stops.campa: Princeton University Press publishes six hundred and twenty-five pages by von Neumann and the Viennese economist Oskar Morgenstern, who came to the Institute in 1938 and found in residence the man whose 1928 theorem he had been citing. The book axiomatises rational choice: utility built out of preferences over gambles, coalitions, the value of a game to each player who plays it. A second edition in 1947 derives expected utility from the axioms. Economics receives it slowly, and then entirely.
stops.quote: I think that it is a relatively good approximation to truth ... that mathematical ideas originate in empirics. But, once they are conceived, the subject begins to live a peculiar life of its own and is ... governed by almost entirely aesthetical motivations.
stops.quote_source: John von Neumann, 'The Mathematician', in The Works of the Mind, ed. R. B. Heywood (Chicago: University of Chicago Press, 1947); ellipses mark cuts in the original sentence
suggested_refs: Theory of Games and Economic Behavior, Princeton University Press, 1944; second edition 1947; sixtieth anniversary edition 2004
sources: Wikipedia, 'Theory of Games and Economic Behavior'

stops.name: Philadelphia, the First Draft of a Report on the EDVAC
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1945; the thirtieth of June is the conventional date given for the circulated draft
stops.campa: Goldstine mimeographs a hundred and one pages titled First Draft of a Report on the EDVAC. It describes a machine in five parts, arithmetic, control, memory, input, output, with program and data held in the same store, and it describes them in the language of idealised neurons rather than of vacuum tubes, so that the design floats free of the hardware. The draft is unfinished, it cites nobody, and it carries one name on the cover. Eckert and Mauchly's patent claims die of it.
stops.quote: What we are creating now is a monster whose influence is going to change history, provided there is any history left... yet it would be impossible not to see it through.
stops.quote_source: Klara Dan von Neumann, unpublished memoir 'Grasshopper in Very Tall Grass', ch. 7, c. 1962-63, Library of Congress MSS 99600, Box 56; quoted in Dyson, Turing's Cathedral. Her recollection of a night in early 1945, not his own writing
suggested_refs: First Draft of a Report on the EDVAC, mimeographed by the Moore School, June 1945

stops.name: Princeton, the machine built at the Institute
stops.date_confidence: attested: construction from 1946, fully operational on 10 June 1952. The 1946 start month is not documented and is defaulted
stops.campa: The Institute puts up a building it did not want, for a project it thought beneath a school with no laboratories, and construction begins on a machine of forty bits in parallel with a memory of one thousand and twenty-four words held on cathode-ray tubes. It is fully operational on the tenth of June 1952. Its first serious job is a hydrogen bomb calculation and its second is the first numerical weather forecast ever computed. Klára von Neumann writes code for it. The design is given away free.
stops.quote: Von Neumann was a great mathematician and had the reputation at that time of being the cleverest man in the world. He was supposed to be the intellectual force driving the whole development of computers.
stops.quote_source: Freeman Dyson, Infinite in All Directions (New York: Harper & Row, 1988), p. 182
suggested_refs: The IAS machine, Princeton, 1946-1958, and the copies built from its published design

stops.name: Murray Hill, a name for the uncertainty function
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the conversation is undated, reaches print only in 1971, and is reported by Shannon through third parties. The year here is a placeholder inside the c. 1940-48 bracket the corpus already carries
stops.campa: Claude Shannon, at Bell Laboratories, has a function that measures how much of a message is not yet known and no name to put on it. The story, undated and printed only decades afterward, is that he asks von Neumann and is told to call it entropy on two grounds, the second of which is that nobody knows what entropy is and he will therefore always win the argument. Betty Shannon runs the entropy of English by hand in the same house. Shannon held a fellowship at the Institute in 1940 and knew whom to ask.
stops.quote: You should call it entropy, for two reasons. In the first place your uncertainty function has been used in statistical mechanics under that name, so it already has a name. In the second place, and more important, no one really knows what entropy really is, so in a debate you will always have the advantage.
stops.quote_source: Reported by Claude Shannon in Myron Tribus and Edward C. McIrvine, 'Energy and Information', Scientific American 225, no. 3 (September 1971), p. 180. Secondhand, undated, and commonly misquoted as saying thermodynamics
suggested_refs: Tribus and McIrvine, 'Energy and Information', Scientific American, September 1971, p. 180

stops.name: Santa Monica, the game with no communication
stops.date_confidence: inferred: the RAND consultancy is attested across the late 1940s and the 1950s without a start date, and 1948 is a placeholder inside that bracket
stops.campa: He consults for the RAND Corporation in Santa Monica, where the mathematics of the 1944 book is being turned into planning for a war nobody has fought. Two-person zero-sum games have a value; the strategic position between two nuclear powers does not, and the men in the building learn the difference from the prisoner's dilemma, formulated at RAND in 1950 by Flood and Dresher. His theorem is the floor of the discipline, and the awkward cases that break it are built on top of it.
suggested_refs: The RAND Corporation mathematics division, Santa Monica, and the 1950 Flood-Dresher experiment

stops.name: Washington, the state of sin
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 1951 volume; month and day not documented and defaulted. The essay itself is not freely hosted and was verified through Wikiquote's full publication citation rather than fetched
stops.campa: The National Bureau of Standards prints his contribution to a symposium volume on the Monte Carlo method, the technique he and Stanislaw Ulam developed at Los Alamos: solve a deterministic problem by simulating a great many random ones. The machines have no source of randomness and must manufacture their random numbers by arithmetic, which is to say deterministically. He puts the objection into one sentence and then goes on using the method, because there is nothing else to use.
stops.quote: Any one who considers arithmetical methods of producing random digits is, of course, in a state of sin.
stops.quote_source: John von Neumann, 'Various Techniques Used in Connection with Random Digits', in Monte Carlo Method, National Bureau of Standards Applied Mathematics Series 12 (Washington: GPO, 1951)
suggested_refs: Monte Carlo Method, NBS Applied Mathematics Series 12, 1951
sources: Wikiquote, 'John von Neumann', with full publication citation

stops.name: Cambridge, the International Congress of Mathematicians
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1950; the month is inferred from the congress calendar and the day is not documented
stops.campa: He addresses the International Congress of Mathematicians at Cambridge, Massachusetts, the first congress held in the United States since 1893 and the first held anywhere since the war. He is also, that year, a member of the Armed Forces Special Weapons Project. The two functions sit in one diary without friction. In 1951 the American Mathematical Society elects him its president, and he serves the term while chairing committees whose minutes stay classified for decades afterward.
suggested_refs: Proceedings of the International Congress of Mathematicians, Cambridge, Massachusetts, 1950

stops.name: Washington, the Teapot Committee
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1953-55; month and day not documented and defaulted
stops.campa: He chairs the Strategic Missile Evaluation Committee, which the men on it call the Teapot Committee, and it reports that a thermonuclear warhead can be built light enough for a rocket to carry across an ocean. The Atlas programme is reordered around that sentence and given the highest national priority. The committee's arithmetic is the reason the intercontinental ballistic missile exists on the schedule it does. He is by now consulting for the Air Force, the Navy, the Army, and the Commission at once.
suggested_refs: Report of the Strategic Missile Evaluation Committee (the Teapot Committee), 1954

stops.name: Washington, the Oppenheimer hearing
stops.date_confidence: attested for April 1954; the day of his own testimony is not fixed here
stops.campa: The Atomic Energy Commission's personnel security board sits in a converted office and takes Robert Oppenheimer's clearance away from him. Von Neumann testifies for him, and does it as a man who stood on the other side of the hydrogen bomb argument in 1949 and says so: the judgment was honest, the men who made it were not disloyal, and a scientist asked to advise cannot be tried afterward for the advice. The board revokes the clearance anyway. Eleven months later von Neumann is sworn in as a commissioner of the body that took it.
suggested_refs: In the Matter of J. Robert Oppenheimer: Transcript of Hearing before Personnel Security Board, April-May 1954

stops.name: Amsterdam, the last congress
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1954; the congress opened on 2 September and the specific day of his address is not fixed here
stops.campa: He addresses the congress at Amsterdam, and it is the last time the international mathematical community sees him on his feet in front of it. He is fifty years old. He has been president of the American Mathematical Society, has a machine running at Princeton with his logic inside it, and holds clearances that keep half his working week out of any proceedings whatever. Within seven months he will be nominated to the Atomic Energy Commission and will say that accepting it ends his scientific life.
stops.quote: The sciences do not try to explain, they hardly even try to interpret, they mainly make models. By a model is meant a mathematical construct which, with the addition of certain verbal interpretations, describes observed phenomena. The justification of such a mathematical construct is solely and precisely that it is expected to work.
stops.quote_source: John von Neumann, 'Method in the Physical Sciences', in The Unity of Knowledge, ed. L. G. Leary (New York: Doubleday, 1955), p. 157; the collection itself was not fetched and the citation comes through Wikiquote
suggested_refs: Proceedings of the International Congress of Mathematicians, Amsterdam, 1954

stops.name: Washington, sworn in to the Atomic Energy Commission
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: Eisenhower nominates him, the Senate confirms him, and he is sworn in as a commissioner of the Atomic Energy Commission. He moves to Washington, resigns nothing at Princeton on paper and abandons all of it in practice, and takes a post that will consume every working hour he has left. He accepts it, he tells friends, because the alternative is that the seat is filled by a man who cannot read the calculations. He is fifty-one, and he holds the office until the day he dies.
stops.quote: For progress there is no cure. Any attempt to find automatically safe channels for the present explosive variety of progress must lead to frustration. The only safety possible is relative, and it lies in an intelligent exercise of day-to-day judgment.
stops.quote_source: John von Neumann, 'Can We Survive Technology?', Fortune, June 1955; reprinted in Collected Works, ed. A. H. Taub, vol. VI, 504-519. Wikiquote's 1950 dating is an uncorrected error
suggested_refs: The United States Atomic Energy Commission, commissioners' records, 1955-1957

stops.name: Washington, the mass at the collarbone
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1955; the month is a placeholder within the year
stops.campa: A mass is found near his collarbone and the biopsy comes back malignant. Whether the cause was the radiation he stood near at Trinity and at the Pacific tests is repeated in every account of his death and established in none of them; the men around him believed it, and belief is what the record holds. The disease is already metastatic when it is found. He continues to sit on the Commission, is driven to meetings, and calculates in his head at the pace everyone in the room has always described.
suggested_refs: The 1955 diagnosis and the recurring claim of radiation exposure at Trinity and the Pacific tests

stops.name: Washington, the Medal of Freedom
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day by the citation itself. Not a bedside presentation: the date precedes his admission to Walter Reed by two months. Not the Presidential Medal of Freedom either, which did not exist until Kennedy created it in 1963
stops.campa: Eisenhower presents him with the Medal of Freedom, the decoration Truman created in 1945; the Presidential Medal of Freedom that later takes over the name will not exist until 1963. The citation is dated the fifteenth of February. He receives it in a wheelchair, two months before he is admitted to Walter Reed, and the widely repeated picture of a bedside presentation is not what happened. The Commission carries him on its books as a sitting member throughout.
suggested_refs: American Presidency Project, 'Citation Accompanying Medal of Freedom Presented to Dr. John von Neumann', 15 February 1956

stops.name: Walter Reed, the first Fermi Award
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1956 as the award's first year; the month is placed at his admission to Walter Reed and the day is not documented
stops.campa: He is admitted to Walter Reed and does not leave it. The Atomic Energy Commission gives him the Enrico Fermi Award and he is the first person ever to receive it; the presentation is made by Lewis Strauss, the chairman, and not by the President, and the accounts that bundle it together with the Medal of Freedom are wrong on both counts. Officers with clearances sit outside the room in shifts, because of what is in his memory and what he might say under sedation.
suggested_refs: The Enrico Fermi Award of the Atomic Energy Commission, first conferred 1956

stops.name: Walter Reed, the eighth of February
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day. The corpus's canonical Washington hospital pin is used; two coordinates in the gathered material were out by 1.2 km and 4.7 km respectively
stops.campa: He dies at Walter Reed on the eighth of February, fifty-three years old, still a sitting commissioner of the Atomic Energy Commission. He had asked for a priest; Father Anselm Strittmatter attended him, and said afterward that the last rites brought him no comfort and that he remained frightened of death. Wigner wrote that his logic forced him to accept what most men decline to look at. Teller said he had never seen a human being suffer more than von Neumann suffered while his mind went.
stops.quote: I have sometimes wondered whether a brain like von Neumann's does not indicate a species superior to that of man.
stops.quote_source: Hans Bethe, quoted in LIFE magazine, 1957
suggested_refs: Walter Reed Army Medical Center, 6900 Georgia Avenue NW, Washington, D.C.
sources: Bhattacharya, The Man from the Future

segments.name: The Grave, the Books, the Crater

stops.name: Princeton Cemetery, the ground with Godel and Wigner in it
stops.date_confidence: the burial at Princeton Cemetery is attested; the day of interment is a reasonable placeholder and the plot within the cemetery could not be confirmed, FindAGrave memorial 2223 having returned HTTP 403
stops.campa: He is buried at Princeton Cemetery, about two and a half kilometres from the Institute where he held his chair for twenty-four years, in ground that already holds Grover Cleveland and Aaron Burr. Kurt Gödel is buried here in 1978 and Eugene Wigner in 1995: the man who proved Hilbert's programme impossible, the man who wrote the obituary memoir, and the man himself, all inside a few hundred paces. The Institute closes its computer project the year after the funeral.
stops.quote: A mind of von Neumann's inexorable logic had to understand and accept much that most of us do not want to accept and do not even wish to understand.
stops.quote_source: Eugene Wigner, 'John von Neumann (1903-1957)', Year Book of the American Philosophical Society (1958); reprinted in Symmetries and Reflections (1967), p. 261
suggested_refs: Princeton Cemetery, Witherspoon Street, Princeton, New Jersey

stops.name: New Haven, the lectures he could not deliver
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 1958 publication; month and day not documented and defaulted
stops.campa: Yale had invited him to give the Silliman Lectures and he had accepted, and the manuscript is unfinished when he dies. Yale University Press publishes it in 1958 as The Computer and the Brain, with a preface by Klára Dán von Neumann. It sets the arithmetic of a machine beside the arithmetic of a nervous system and concludes that the brain does not use any language the mathematics then existing would recognise. It is reissued in 2000 and again in 2012, each time with a foreword arguing that it predicted the present.
suggested_refs: The Computer and the Brain, Yale University Press, 1958; reissues of 2000 and 2012

stops.name: Mountain View, the machine named for him
stops.date_confidence: attested: JOHNNIAC built 1953, decommissioned 1966, nearly scrapped in 1989, now held at the Computer History Museum. Month and day of decommissioning not documented
stops.campa: The RAND Corporation built a copy of the Princeton machine in 1953, called it JOHNNIAC for John von Neumann Numerical Integrator and Automatic Computer, and asked his permission for the name. It is retired in 1966 after thirteen years of service. In 1989 it is found abandoned in a museum parking lot and rescued, and it now stands in the Computer History Museum at Mountain View. The Princeton machine it was copied from had been shut down in 1958; the copy outlasted the original by eight years.
stops.quote: He was the cleverest man I ever knew, without exception.
stops.quote_source: Jacob Bronowski, The Ascent of Man (British Broadcasting Corporation, 1974)
suggested_refs: JOHNNIAC, Computer History Museum, Mountain View, California

stops.name: The Moon, a walled plain on the far side
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 1970 IAU naming; month and day are not applicable and are defaulted
stops.campa: The International Astronomical Union gives his name to a walled plain on the far side of the Moon, seventy-five kilometres across at forty degrees north and a hundred and fifty-three east, ground no human eye had seen until a Soviet probe photographed it in 1959. Before the naming it was called Crater 58. The far side is the half of the Moon that never turns toward the Earth, and the naming comes thirteen years after his death. Asteroid 22824 carries the name as well.
suggested_refs: Von Neumann crater, lunar far side, 40 17 N 153 15 E, diameter 74.83 km, named 1970
sources: Wikipedia, 'List of things named after John von Neumann'

stops.name: Kecskemet, the nation takes the name back
stops.date_confidence: attested for 2016; month and day not documented and defaulted
stops.campa: Hungary merges a college and a technical institute at Kecskemét and calls the result Neumann János Egyetem. The country claims back a mathematician who left it at seventeen, published in German, took American citizenship at thirty-three, and died a commissioner of the United States Atomic Energy Commission. The gymnasium on Városligeti fasor still stands and still teaches. Wigner, Teller, and von Neumann came out of the same few streets of Budapest, and none of the three came back.
suggested_refs: Neumann Janos Egyetem, Kecskemet, established 2016
sources: Wikipedia, 'List of things named after John von Neumann'
